articles.title: First for RNA therapy: man with rare motor-neuron disease improves after treatment
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 18 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02945-zGene-targeting treatments could be used to treat other people with rare forms of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
articles.content:
Physicist Stephen Hawking lived with motor neuron disease for longer than any other person known.Credit: Santi Visalli/Getty

A man with an uncommon type of motor neuron disease experienced improved symptoms and continued to work as a physician a year after becoming the first person to receive a drug designed to target the specific genetic mutation that causes his disease1. Researchers say the early results are exciting and lay the foundation for more treatments for neurodegenerative diseases caused by rare mutations.

The man had a slowly progressing form of motor neuron disease, also called amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), caused by a rare mutation that leads to protein build-up that contributes to the death of motor neurons. He received an RNA treatment called antisense oligonucleotide therapy. Unlike typical gene therapy, which alters a person’s genes to treat a genetic disease, antisense oligonucleotide therapy, uses short strands of genetic material to target RNA produced by the gene and reduce how much protein is made. The results are published in Med this week.

Steve Vucic, a neurologist and ALS researcher at the University of Sydney in Australia, says the results are an “exciting first step”, although it is too early to know whether the treatment could stop disease progression or be a cure. That will require monitoring the trial participant for another two or three years and testing the drug in more people.

Similar antisense oligonucleotide therapies are the future of treatment for many people with ALS, says Fleur Garton, a neurological disease researcher at the University of Queensland in Brisbane, Australia. Roughly 5–10% of people with ALS have a known genetic mutation. Antisense therapies seem to be safe and can be developed for people with common genetic mutations, for those with rare or even unique mutations, and for people whose disease is caused by multiple mutations, she adds.

Early encouragement

ALS causes motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord to die, leading to symptoms such as muscle weakness, difficulty speaking and progressive paralysis. Most people with the condition eventually require a ventilator to breathe, and death is often caused by respiratory failure. There is no cure and treatment options are limited; The average life expectancy after diagnosis is about two to five years.

The trial participant’s disease is caused by a mutation in the gene CHCHD10, found in fewer than 1% of people who inherit ALS. This gene encodes a protein that enables mitochondria — the organelles that generate the energy needed to power cells — to function properly. Defects in the gene can damage the mitochondria and are thought to contribute to the death of neurons.

The patient received three 50-milligram doses of the drug in his spine, followed by three 75-milligram doses, between April 2024 and April 2025. He did not experience any serious negative side effects, the authors reported. He also showed no signs of cognitive decline, a common symptom of ALS.

A year after the first dose, his blood levels of neurofilament light chain proteins — which are produced by damaged neurons, and so are used as a biomarker for ALS progression — had reduced to the normal reference range. Vucic says this suggests that the treatment could be preserving the neurons in the man’s brain.

Scores on a test that measures motor skills, breathing and neurological function had improved, and other scores for breathing and cognition remained stable. Some people with ALS experience short-term improvements in symptoms without treatment, although study co-author Björn Oskarrson, a neurologist at Mayo Clinic in Jacksonville, Florida, says that sustained improvement without treatment is rare.

Antisense therapies have been developed to target more common gene mutations that cause ALS, but those therapies took at least a decade to make. By contrast, the drug that targets CHCHD10 took only three years to develop, says Oskarrson. Being able to develop a drug to target a specific person’s mutation, test it in animals and then give it to the person within their lifespan was amazing, he adds.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a groundbreaking medical treatment using RNA antisense oligonucleotide therapy that improved symptoms in a man with a rare form of ALS, a typically fatal neurodegenerative disease. This represents a significant breakthrough with broad implications for treating genetic forms of ALS and potentially other neurodegenerative diseases. The treatment shows tangible, measurable benefits, including symptom improvement and biomarker normalization, and the rapid development timeline highlights innovation in personalized medicine.
articles.personality_title: New RNA therapy improves symptoms in man with rare motor neuron disease
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a disease that damages motor neurons, causing muscle weakness and paralysis. Most people with ALS live only a few years after diagnosis. A rare form of ALS is caused by genetic mutations that lead to harmful protein build-up in nerve cells.

**What happened** – A man with a rare genetic form of ALS became the first person to receive an RNA-based treatment called antisense oligonucleotide therapy. This therapy targets the RNA from the faulty gene to reduce harmful protein production. Between April 2024 and April 2025, he received six doses of the drug injected into his spine. A year after starting treatment, his symptoms improved and tests showed fewer signs of nerve damage.

**Impact** – This is the first time RNA therapy has shown clear benefits for a person with a rare form of ALS. Unlike traditional gene therapy, this treatment works by targeting RNA, offering a new way to treat diseases caused by specific genetic mutations. The patient did not have serious side effects and even kept working as a doctor. The treatment was developed in just three years, much faster than usual, showing the potential for personalized medicine.

**What's next step** – Researchers will continue to monitor the patient for the next two to three years to see if the benefits last and if the disease progression stops. They also plan to test this therapy on more people with ALS caused by different genetic mutations. This could lead to new treatments tailored to each patient’s unique genetic cause.

**One-sentence takeaway** – RNA-based antisense therapy has safely improved symptoms in a man with a rare genetic form of ALS, opening new paths for personalized treatments of neurodegenerative diseases.

articles.personality_title_es: Nueva terapia de ARN mejora síntomas en hombre con rara enfermedad de motoneurona
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La esclerosis lateral amiotrófica (ELA) es una enfermedad que destruye las motoneuronas, causando debilidad muscular y parálisis. La mayoría de las personas con ELA viven solo unos años después del diagnóstico. Una forma rara de ELA es causada por mutaciones genéticas que provocan acumulación dañina de proteínas en las células nerviosas.

**Qué pasó** – Un hombre con una forma rara de ELA causada por un gen defectuoso fue la primera persona en recibir un tratamiento basado en ARN llamado terapia con oligonucleótidos antisentido. Este tratamiento actúa sobre el ARN producido por el gen defectuoso para reducir la producción de proteínas dañinas. Entre abril de 2024 y abril de 2025, recibió seis dosis inyectadas en la columna vertebral. Un año después, sus síntomas mejoraron y las pruebas mostraron menos daño en los nervios.

**Impacto** – Es la primera vez que una terapia de ARN muestra beneficios claros en una persona con una forma rara de ELA. A diferencia de la terapia genética tradicional, este tratamiento actúa sobre el ARN, ofreciendo una nueva forma de tratar enfermedades causadas por mutaciones genéticas específicas. El paciente no tuvo efectos secundarios graves y pudo seguir trabajando como médico. El tratamiento se desarrolló en solo tres años, mucho más rápido de lo usual, mostrando el potencial de la medicina personalizada.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores seguirán controlando al paciente durante dos o tres años para ver si los beneficios continúan y si la enfermedad deja de avanzar. También planean probar esta terapia en más personas con ELA causada por diferentes mutaciones genéticas. Esto podría llevar a tratamientos personalizados para cada causa genética.

**Frase clave** – La terapia antisense basada en ARN mejoró de forma segura los síntomas de un hombre con una forma rara de ELA, abriendo nuevas vías para tratamientos personalizados de enfermedades neurodegenerativas.

articles.title: Scientists restore a brain protein and reverse signs of aging in mice
articles.summary: Scientists found that declining levels of the brain protein Menin may help drive aging, with lower levels in mice linked to inflammation, cognitive decline, weaker bones, and thinner skin. Restoring Menin reversed several age-related changes, while the amino acid D-serine improved cognition, hinting at a potentially intriguing new target for healthy aging.
articles.content:
Memory problems, thinning skin, and declining bone mass may seem like separate consequences of growing older. Yet experiments in mice suggest that changes in a protein deep inside the brain can influence all three. Restoring that protein, called Menin, improved several signs of aging, while a separate treatment with the amino acid D-serine improved cognition.

The findings came from a study published on March 16, 2023, in the open access journal PLOS Biology, led by Lige Leng of Xiamen University in Xiamen, China, and colleagues. The work identified a possible connection between brain inflammation, metabolism, and aging throughout the body. Research published since then has added to that picture, while also showing why the supplement findings require careful interpretation.

How a Brain Protein Could Influence Aging

The researchers focused on the hypothalamus, a small brain region that helps coordinate metabolism and other essential functions. It also appears to influence how the body ages. As inflammatory signaling increases in this region, it can contribute to changes both within the brain and in tissues elsewhere in the body.

Before the 2023 study, Leng and colleagues had found that Menin helps restrain inflammation in the hypothalamus. That raised an important question: Could losing some of this protection help set age-related decline in motion?

The team found that Menin levels fell with age in certain neurons within the ventromedial hypothalamus, an area involved in regulating metabolism. The same decline was not seen in astrocytes and microglia, two types of cells that support and protect the brain. This suggested that the change was specific to particular cells rather than a uniform loss across the region.

To investigate whether Menin loss could actually contribute to aging, rather than simply accompany it, the researchers created conditional knockout mice. These animals were genetically engineered so that Menin could be selectively removed. Reducing Menin in younger mice increased hypothalamic inflammation and brought on several aging-related traits, including lower bone mass, thinner skin, cognitive decline, and a modestly shorter lifespan.

The D-Serine Connection

Menin loss also disrupted a chemical pathway important for communication between brain cells. Mice with less Menin had lower levels of D-serine, an amino acid that helps activate receptors involved in learning and memory. These receptors help neurons adjust the strength of their connections, a process essential for storing information.

An enzyme involved in D-serine production (which was in turn regulated by Menin) became less active, reducing the amino acid's supply. The findings suggested that Menin could influence cognition not only through inflammation, but also by helping maintain the chemistry that supports brain signaling.

D-serine is sometimes used as a dietary supplement, but an important distinction can get lost in discussions of food sources. Serine occurs in foods such as soybeans, eggs, fish, and nuts, while the form incorporated into dietary proteins is L-serine. The body can convert L-serine into D-serine, but the two forms are not interchangeable, and eating these foods is not equivalent to receiving the experimental D-serine treatment.

Restoring Menin in Older Mice

The researchers next tested whether raising Menin levels could improve the condition of elderly (20-month-old) mice. They delivered the gene for Menin into the hypothalamus, allowing cells in that region to produce more of the protein.

Thirty days later, the treated mice had improvements in skin thickness and bone mass, along with better performance on tests of learning, cognition, and balance. The changes were accompanied by higher D-serine levels in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. The study also reported that restoring Menin extended lifespan in the treated mice.

A separate experiment tested a simpler approach: giving mice D-serine in their drinking water for three weeks. This improved cognitive performance, including in older animals. However, the supplement did not reproduce the broader improvements in physical aging traits seen after Menin restoration. The distinction matters: the study did not show that taking D-serine reversed aging throughout the body.

At the time, Leng described the potential significance of the findings:

"We speculate that the decline of Menin expression in the hypothalamus with age may be one of the driving factors of aging, and Menin may be the key protein connecting the genetic, inflammatory, and metabolic factors of aging. D-serine is a potentially promising therapeutic for cognitive decline."

Leng added, "Ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) Menin signaling diminished in aged mice, which contributes to systemic aging phenotypes and cognitive deficits. The effects of Menin on aging are mediated by neuroinflammatory changes and metabolic pathway signaling, accompanied by serine deficiency in VMH, while restoration of Menin in VMH reversed aging-related phenotypes."

What Later Research Has Added

Subsequent studies have explored related mechanisms, although they should not be treated as direct confirmation of the entire Menin aging pathway.

A study published in the Journal of Physiology and Biochemistry in March 2024 examined Menin in cultured mouse hippocampal cells exposed to the stress hormone corticosterone. A compound called itaconate increased Menin levels and reduced inflammation and a form of cell death. When the researchers silenced Menin, that protection disappeared. The result supported a protective role for Menin in another experimental setting, but it was a cell study, not a demonstration of slower aging in animals or people.

Other work has strengthened the case that communication between the hypothalamus and the rest of the body can influence aging. In a 2024 Cell Metabolism study, researchers at Washington University School of Medicine identified a different group of hypothalamic neurons that communicates with fat tissue. Interventions that maintained or stimulated this system increased physical activity and extended lifespan in mice. The study involved a different molecular pathway from Menin, but reinforced the broader idea that brain signals can affect aging beyond the brain.

A much larger view emerged in January 2025, when an Allen Institute team reported an analysis of roughly 1.2 million mouse brain cells in Nature. Some of the cell types most sensitive to aging were concentrated around the hypothalamus's third ventricle, a fluid-filled cavity. Many showed reduced activity in genes associated with neuronal function alongside increased activity in genes related to immune responses. That study mapped changes associated with aging rather than testing a treatment, but it highlighted the hypothalamus as an important area for further investigation.

Why More D-Serine Is Not Necessarily Better

Later research also complicates the idea that increasing D-serine should always benefit an aging brain.

In April 2025, a study in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences examined mice engineered to develop features of Alzheimer's disease. In that model, an early rise in D-serine accompanied disruptions in brain signaling. Genetically removing the enzyme that produces D-serine prevented or reduced several later cognitive problems. This was a different biological setting from the Menin experiments, but it demonstrated that D-serine can have different effects depending on the underlying disease process.

Research published on September 16, 2026, in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease pointed in another direction. In a different Alzheimer's mouse model, a diet enriched with L-serine increased blood levels of both L-serine and D-serine and partially restored measures of new neuron production in the hippocampus. It did not improve the buildup of amyloid, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease. Importantly, this experiment tested L-serine and the production of new neurons, not D-serine supplementation as a treatment for human aging.

Taken together, these findings suggest that serine metabolism is a promising research target, but not a simple case of more being better. The form of serine, the condition being studied, and the outcome being measured all matter. Neither study directly confirms or overturns the original Menin results.

What the Findings Mean for People

There is some human research on D-serine, although it does not establish an aging treatment. A small randomized study published in 2016, before the Menin work, tested a single dose in 50 healthy older adults. Participants improved on one measure of a computerized maze task, but the researchers found no significant benefit on the other cognitive tests or mood measures. The experiment did not establish lasting memory benefits, slower aging, or the safety of prolonged use in older adults.

The Menin findings leave several important questions unresolved. Researchers still need to determine what causes the protein to decline with age, how much of the resulting physical and cognitive deterioration can be prevented, and how long any benefits might last. They also need to understand whether altering Menin or supplementing D-serine could produce unintended effects.

The central possibility remains compelling: some changes associated with aging may be influenced by signals originating in a small part of the brain. Understanding those signals could reveal ways to protect function later in life. For now, however, the evidence points to an experimental pathway worth investigating, not a supplement proven to turn back human aging.

This discovery has broad implications for understanding and potentially treating aging in humans, representing a meaningful advance in health research with substantial positive impact. The article provides detailed context on the study, mechanisms involved, and subsequent related research, fulfilling the criteria for inspiring good news.
articles.personality_title: Restoring a brain protein reverses aging signs in mice
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have been studying how aging affects the body, including memory loss, thinner skin, and weaker bones. Recent research suggests that changes in a small part of the brain might play a big role in these age-related problems.

**What happened** – In a study published in 2023, researchers led by Lige Leng found that levels of a brain protein called Menin drop as mice get older. Menin is found in a brain area called the hypothalamus, which controls metabolism and other body functions. When Menin was removed from young mice, they showed signs of aging like weaker bones, thinner skin, and memory problems. Then, the scientists restored Menin in old mice and saw improvements in these areas, along with better learning and longer life. They also gave mice a supplement called D-serine, which helped with memory but did not improve other aging signs.

**Impact** – This study shows that a single brain protein can affect many parts of the body as animals age. It connects brain inflammation and metabolism to aging symptoms. The findings suggest new ways to study aging and possibly develop treatments that protect the brain and body. Unlike some treatments that only target one symptom, Menin restoration improved several age-related issues at once.

**What's next step** – Scientists need to learn why Menin levels drop with age and whether similar effects happen in humans. More research will explore if boosting Menin or using D-serine supplements can safely help people maintain memory and physical health as they get older. Researchers also want to understand if these treatments might have side effects or work differently depending on health conditions.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Restoring the brain protein Menin in mice reversed multiple aging signs, pointing to new directions for understanding and possibly treating age-related decline in the future.
articles.personality_title_fr: La restauration d'une protéine cérébrale inverse les signes du vieillissement chez la souris
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques étudient comment le vieillissement affecte le corps, notamment la perte de mémoire, la peau qui s'amincit et la fragilité des os. Des recherches récentes suggèrent que des changements dans une petite partie du cerveau pourraient jouer un rôle important dans ces problèmes liés à l'âge.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Dans une étude publiée en 2023, des chercheurs dirigés par Lige Leng ont découvert que les niveaux d'une protéine cérébrale appelée Menin diminuent avec l'âge chez la souris. Menin se trouve dans une zone du cerveau appelée hypothalamus, qui contrôle le métabolisme et d'autres fonctions du corps. Lorsque Menin a été supprimée chez de jeunes souris, elles ont montré des signes de vieillissement comme des os plus faibles, une peau plus fine et des problèmes de mémoire. Ensuite, les scientifiques ont restauré Menin chez des souris âgées et ont observé des améliorations dans ces domaines, ainsi qu'une meilleure capacité d'apprentissage et une vie plus longue. Ils ont aussi donné aux souris un supplément appelé D-sérine, qui a aidé à la mémoire mais pas aux autres signes de vieillissement.

**Impact** – Cette étude montre qu'une seule protéine cérébrale peut influencer plusieurs parties du corps lors du vieillissement. Elle relie l'inflammation du cerveau et le métabolisme aux symptômes du vieillissement. Ces résultats suggèrent de nouvelles pistes pour étudier le vieillissement et développer des traitements qui protègent le cerveau et le corps. Contrairement à certains traitements qui ne ciblent qu'un symptôme, la restauration de Menin a amélioré plusieurs problèmes liés à l'âge en même temps.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques doivent comprendre pourquoi les niveaux de Menin diminuent avec l'âge et si des effets similaires se produisent chez l'humain. De nouvelles recherches exploreront si augmenter Menin ou utiliser des suppléments de D-sérine peut aider en toute sécurité les personnes à maintenir leur mémoire et leur santé physique en vieillissant. Ils veulent aussi savoir si ces traitements peuvent avoir des effets secondaires ou fonctionner différemment selon les conditions de santé.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Restaurer la protéine cérébrale Menin chez la souris a inversé plusieurs signes du vieillissement, ouvrant de nouvelles voies pour comprendre et peut-être traiter le déclin lié à l'âge à l'avenir.
articles.personality_title_es: Restaurar una proteína cerebral revierte signos de envejecimiento en ratones
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos han estado estudiando cómo el envejecimiento afecta el cuerpo, incluyendo la pérdida de memoria, el adelgazamiento de la piel y el debilitamiento de los huesos. Investigaciones recientes sugieren que cambios en una pequeña parte del cerebro podrían tener un papel importante en estos problemas relacionados con la edad.

**Qué pasó** – En un estudio publicado en 2023, investigadores liderados por Lige Leng encontraron que los niveles de una proteína cerebral llamada Menin disminuyen a medida que los ratones envejecen. Menin se encuentra en una zona del cerebro llamada hipotálamo, que controla el metabolismo y otras funciones del cuerpo. Cuando se eliminó Menin en ratones jóvenes, mostraron signos de envejecimiento como huesos más débiles, piel más fina y problemas de memoria. Luego, los científicos restauraron Menin en ratones viejos y observaron mejoras en estas áreas, junto con mejor aprendizaje y mayor vida. También les dieron un suplemento llamado D-serina, que ayudó con la memoria pero no mejoró otros signos de envejecimiento.

**Impacto** – Este estudio muestra que una sola proteína cerebral puede afectar muchas partes del cuerpo durante el envejecimiento. Conecta la inflamación cerebral y el metabolismo con los síntomas del envejecimiento. Los hallazgos sugieren nuevas formas de estudiar el envejecimiento y posibles tratamientos para proteger el cerebro y el cuerpo. A diferencia de algunos tratamientos que solo atacan un síntoma, la restauración de Menin mejoró varios problemas relacionados con la edad al mismo tiempo.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos necesitan entender por qué los niveles de Menin bajan con la edad y si efectos similares ocurren en humanos. Más investigaciones explorarán si aumentar Menin o usar suplementos de D-serina puede ayudar de forma segura a las personas a mantener la memoria y la salud física a medida que envejecen. También quieren saber si estos tratamientos podrían tener efectos secundarios o funcionar diferente según la salud de cada persona.

**Resumen en una frase** – Restaurar la proteína cerebral Menin en ratones revirtió varios signos de envejecimiento, señalando nuevas direcciones para entender y posiblemente tratar el declive relacionado con la edad en el futuro.

articles.title: Scientists discover cells that cheat death and rebuild damaged tissue
articles.summary: Scientists discovered a population of cells that can start the process of programmed cell death, survive it, and then help rapidly rebuild damaged tissue. Their descendants become far more resistant to future damage, revealing a mechanism that could improve healing but may also help cancers return after treatment.
articles.content:
Scientists uncover a cellular survival mechanism that helps severely damaged tissue regenerate and may also reveal why some cancers return after treatment.

Tissues such as skin, along with the epithelial layers that cover and line many organs, have a remarkable ability to rebuild themselves after extensive damage. Scientists have known about this response, called compensatory proliferation, for roughly half a century. Yet exactly how cells manage to trigger such dramatic regrowth has remained a mystery.

The phenomenon was first documented in the 1970s, when researchers exposed fly larvae to high doses of radiation. Despite major damage to epithelial tissue, the larvae were able to regenerate fully functional wings. Similar regenerative responses have since been observed across many species, including humans.

Now, researchers at the Weizmann Institute of Science say they have identified a molecular mechanism that helps explain how this process works. Their study, published in Nature Communications, points to a surprising role for caspases, enzymes best known for helping destroy cells.

Instead of simply promoting cell death, caspases can apparently help certain cells become resistant to death. Those survivors can then participate in rebuilding damaged tissue and may even become better equipped to withstand future injury. The same ability, however, could have a dangerous downside. Cancer cells may exploit this survival mechanism, potentially contributing to tumors that return in a more aggressive and treatment-resistant form.

The discovery could eventually help researchers develop approaches that encourage healthy tissue repair while also reducing the risk of cancer recurrence.

When Cell Death Machinery Promotes Survival

One of the main ways the body eliminates unwanted cells is through apoptosis, a carefully controlled form of cellular "suicide." Cells can enter apoptosis when they become old, damaged, or receive molecular signals telling them that their time is up.

The process involves several caspase enzymes. An initiator caspase first activates the pathway, followed by effector caspases that break apart proteins inside the doomed cell.

During the past two decades, however, researchers have discovered that apoptotic caspases are not limited to killing cells. Work by scientists around the world, including the laboratory of Prof. Eli Arama in Weizmann's Molecular Genetics Department, has shown that these enzymes can also participate in biological processes that are essential for life.

Arama, an early researcher of these nonlethal caspase functions, suspected that they might also help drive compensatory proliferation.

Finding Cells That Start To Die but Survive

To investigate, a team led by Dr. Tslil Braun from Arama's lab recreated the classic experiment that originally revealed compensatory proliferation. The researchers exposed fruit fly larvae to ionizing radiation, but this time they used modern genetic tools to follow the regeneration of epithelial tissue in far greater detail.

"We set out to identify cells that push the self-destruct button but survive anyway," Braun explains. "To do this, we used a delayed sensor that reported on cells in which the initiator caspase had been activated but that nevertheless survived the irradiation. This is how we discovered a population of cells we named DARE cells. Not only did these cells survive the irradiation - they multiplied, repaired the damaged tissue and replenished nearly half of it within 48 hours."

The discovery raised another question. If DARE cells accounted for nearly half of the repaired tissue, where did the rest come from?

The researchers found a second group of cells that were also resistant to death. These cells, called NARE cells, differed in one important way: Their initiator caspase had never been activated.

"We identified another population of death-resistant cells, but unlike DARE cells, they showed no activation of the initiator caspase. We called them NARE cells," Braun says. "Although NARE cells ultimately contribute to tissue regeneration, they cannot do it alone: When we removed DARE cells from the system, compensatory proliferation disappeared entirely. We also found that dying cells in the tissue play a role in the burst of regeneration - DARE cells were activated by signals from their dying neighbors."

How DARE Cells Escape Their Death Sentence

The team next investigated why DARE cells could survive radiation levels that caused nearby cells to undergo apoptosis.

They found that the death process begins normally inside DARE cells. The initiator caspase switches on, but the pathway then stalls before the executioner caspases can complete the destruction of the cell.

"We observed that although the initiator caspase is activated in these cells, the cellular death process stops there and does not progress to the next stage," Arama explains. "We suspected that a protein known as a molecular motor was responsible for this - it can tether the initiator caspase to the cell membrane, preventing it from activating the executioner caspases. Indeed, when we silenced this motor protein, DARE cells proceeded to die and tissue regeneration was impaired. Overactivation of the same motor protein has previously been linked to cancerous tumor growth, which suggests that this might be one of the mechanisms that enables cancer cells to evade apoptosis."

That connection is especially important because cancer treatments such as radiation often work by damaging tumor cells enough to trigger their self-destruction.

Surviving Radiation Can Make Cells Harder To Kill

Tumors that return following radiation therapy are often more aggressive and more difficult to treat. The researchers therefore wanted to know whether cells that survived an initial dose of radiation could pass their resistance to future generations of cells.

"We wanted to understand whether resistance to death is inherited by the descendants of death-resistant cells that survived the initial irradiation," Arama says. "We found that when the same tissue is irradiated a second time, the number of cells that die during the first few hours is half that seen after the first irradiation, and most of the dead cells belong to the NARE population. In other words, the descendants of DARE cells were found to be exceptionally resistant - seven times more resistant to cell death than cells in the original tissue. This may help explain why recurrent tumors become more resistant after radiation."

The findings suggest that surviving an initial assault may leave a lasting biological legacy. Descendants of DARE cells were far more difficult to kill than cells in tissue that had never experienced the first radiation exposure.

That trait could be extremely useful when healthy tissue needs to recover from injury. In cancer, however, the same survival advantage could allow dangerous cells to persist despite treatment.

A Feedback Loop Keeps Regeneration Under Control

Rapid regeneration presents another challenge. Cells need to multiply enough to replace what was lost, but that growth must eventually stop. Otherwise, a repair response could turn into uncontrolled proliferation.

In the final stage of the study, researchers uncovered a signaling system between DARE and NARE cells that appears to maintain this balance.

"DARE cells promote the growth of nearby NARE cells, apparently by secreting growth signals," Arama notes. "In turn, NARE cells secrete signals that inhibit the growth of DARE cells. In fact, we've discovered a negative-feedback loop between the two cell populations that prevents overgrowth."

This exchange allows the two cell populations to support regeneration while placing limits on excessive growth.

From Tissue Repair to Cancer Treatment

The experiments were conducted in fruit flies, so additional research will be needed to determine how closely the same mechanisms operate in people. Fruit fly models, however, have repeatedly helped scientists uncover fundamental biological processes that were later found to have important parallels in humans.

"We hope that, as has often been the case with fly models, the knowledge gained here can be translated into an understanding of the mechanisms that balance growth and confer resistance to cell death in human tissues," Arama concludes. "Many cancers originate in epithelial cells that have lost normal growth control, and many traditional cancer treatments aim to cause them to self-destruct through apoptosis. Our findings pave the way for understanding why such treatments sometimes fail and how they could be improved. The results also point toward new ways in which we might be able to accelerate beneficial regeneration of healthy tissue after injury."

The findings therefore highlight two sides of the same biological survival system. A mechanism that allows healthy tissue to recover from devastating damage could potentially be harnessed to improve healing. At the same time, understanding how cancer cells may take advantage of that mechanism could reveal new strategies for preventing tumors from surviving treatment and returning.

Also participating in the study were Naama Afgin, Dr. Lena Sapozhnikov and Dr. Keren Yacobi-Sharon from Weizmann's Molecular Genetics Department; Dr. Ehud Sivan from Weizmann's Life Sciences Core Facilities Department; Prof. Andreas Bergmann from UMass Chan Medical School, Worcester, MA; and Prof. Luis Alberto Baena-Lopez from the Severo Ochoa Molecular Biology Center (CBM), Spain.

Prof. Eli Arama is the incumbent of the Harry Kay Professorial Chair of Cancer Research and head of the Crown Human Genome Center.

articles.personality_title: Scientists find cells that survive death to rebuild damaged tissue
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long known that some tissues, like skin, can heal themselves after serious damage. This healing process, called compensatory proliferation, was first noticed in the 1970s when fly larvae regrew their wings after radiation damage. However, exactly how cells survive and help regrow tissue was not clear.

**What happened** – Researchers at the Weizmann Institute studied fruit fly larvae exposed to radiation and discovered special cells they called DARE cells. These cells start the process of programmed cell death but stop it before dying, allowing them to survive and multiply. They help repair nearly half of the damaged tissue within two days. Another group called NARE cells also help, but only when DARE cells are present. The team found that DARE cells use a protein to block the final step of cell death, which lets them live and work on tissue repair.

**Impact** – This discovery shows a surprising way cells can resist death to help healing. It also explains why some cancer cells might survive treatments like radiation, making tumors harder to kill and more likely to come back. The finding reveals a balance: these special cells help healthy tissue grow but might also allow cancer cells to survive and grow again.

**What's next step** – Scientists will study if this mechanism works the same way in humans. Understanding this process could lead to new treatments that help injured tissues heal faster and improve cancer therapies by stopping harmful cells from surviving treatment.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists found cells that dodge death to repair tissue, a discovery that could improve healing and explain why some cancers resist treatment and return.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des scientifiques découvrent des cellules qui survivent pour réparer les tissus endommagés
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques savent depuis longtemps que certains tissus, comme la peau, peuvent se réparer après de graves dommages. Ce processus de guérison, appelé prolifération compensatoire, a été observé pour la première fois dans les années 1970 lorsque des larves de mouches ont régénéré leurs ailes après une exposition aux radiations. Cependant, le mécanisme exact permettant aux cellules de survivre et de régénérer le tissu restait inconnu.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs de l'Institut Weizmann ont étudié des larves de mouches exposées à des radiations et ont découvert des cellules spéciales qu'ils ont nommées cellules DARE. Ces cellules commencent le processus de mort cellulaire programmée mais l'arrêtent avant de mourir, ce qui leur permet de survivre et de se multiplier. Elles contribuent à réparer près de la moitié du tissu endommagé en deux jours. Un autre groupe, appelé cellules NARE, aide aussi, mais seulement en présence des cellules DARE. L'équipe a découvert que les cellules DARE utilisent une protéine pour bloquer l'étape finale de la mort cellulaire, ce qui leur permet de vivre et de réparer le tissu.

**Impact** – Cette découverte révèle une façon surprenante pour les cellules de résister à la mort afin d'aider la guérison. Elle explique aussi pourquoi certaines cellules cancéreuses peuvent survivre aux traitements comme la radiothérapie, rendant les tumeurs plus difficiles à éliminer et plus susceptibles de revenir. Cela montre un équilibre : ces cellules spéciales aident les tissus sains à croître mais pourraient aussi permettre aux cellules cancéreuses de survivre et de proliférer.

**Prochaines étapes** – Les scientifiques vont étudier si ce mécanisme fonctionne de la même manière chez l'humain. Comprendre ce processus pourrait conduire à de nouveaux traitements qui accélèrent la guérison des tissus blessés et améliorent les thérapies contre le cancer en empêchant les cellules nocives de survivre au traitement.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Des scientifiques ont découvert des cellules qui échappent à la mort pour réparer les tissus, une avancée qui pourrait améliorer la guérison et expliquer pourquoi certains cancers résistent aux traitements et récidivent.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos descubren células que sobreviven para reparar tejidos dañados
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos han sabido durante mucho tiempo que algunos tejidos, como la piel, pueden sanarse después de daños graves. Este proceso de sanación, llamado proliferación compensatoria, se observó por primera vez en la década de 1970 cuando larvas de mosca regeneraron sus alas tras la exposición a radiación. Sin embargo, no se entendía bien cómo las células sobrevivían y ayudaban a reconstruir el tejido.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores del Instituto Weizmann estudiaron larvas de mosca expuestas a radiación y descubrieron células especiales que llamaron células DARE. Estas células inician el proceso de muerte celular programada, pero lo detienen antes de morir, lo que les permite sobrevivir y multiplicarse. Ayudan a reparar casi la mitad del tejido dañado en dos días. Otro grupo llamado células NARE también ayuda, pero solo cuando las células DARE están presentes. El equipo descubrió que las células DARE usan una proteína para bloquear la etapa final de la muerte celular, permitiéndoles vivir y reparar el tejido.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo muestra una forma sorprendente en que las células pueden resistir la muerte para ayudar a la sanación. También explica por qué algunas células cancerosas pueden sobrevivir a tratamientos como la radioterapia, haciendo que los tumores sean más difíciles de eliminar y más propensos a regresar. Revela un equilibrio: estas células especiales ayudan a que los tejidos sanos crezcan, pero también podrían permitir que las células cancerosas sobrevivan y crezcan.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos estudiarán si este mecanismo funciona igual en humanos. Entender este proceso podría llevar a nuevos tratamientos que ayuden a sanar tejidos lesionados más rápido y mejoren las terapias contra el cáncer al evitar que las células dañinas sobrevivan al tratamiento.

**Resumen en una frase** – Científicos descubrieron células que evaden la muerte para reparar tejidos, un hallazgo que podría mejorar la sanación y explicar por qué algunos cánceres resisten el tratamiento y reaparecen.

articles.title: How fast are you ageing? Ask AI
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 17 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02913-7A new system will help scientists to refine large language models for longevity research and clarify ‘biological’ age.
articles.content:
Some individuals have a ‘biological age’ that is younger than their chronological age.Credit: Karen Haibara/AFP/Getty

Understanding why people age — and how to slow that process down — is an obsession that has stretched across millennia, from mythic quests for immortality to modern science’s hunt for drugs that lengthen lifespan.

Now, that quest has entered the AI era.

A report1 published today in Cell unveils a bespoke artificial-intelligence system that aims to turbocharge longevity research. The system introduces large language models (LLMs) that the authors trained on ageing-biology data. It also includes a suite of 17 tasks that can serve as benchmarks to gauge how well these and other LLMs perform on ageing-related projects. Finally, it includes an interface that brings the models and other ageing-related research tools together with AI assistants called agents to aid analyses.

Gene clock predicts time to death in humans — and assesses ‘biological’ age

The authors used their benchmarks to evaluate both their specialist LLMs and much larger cutting-edge commercial models produced by companies including OpenAI and DeepSeek, that are trained on larger, more diverse data sets to handle a broad range of tasks. In many — although not all — of the tests, the LLMs tailored to ageing research outperformed the large LLMs.

“The paper makes a very important contribution to the longevity and ageing field,” says Marinka Zitnik, a computer scientist at Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts, who was not involved in the work. “It can inform the development of next-generation AI models.”

The work also tackles a key question for the field: how can researchers train AI tools to understand ageing when scientists have not yet defined the concept for themselves? “For certain disease areas, such as cancer, the AI tasks can be very crisply defined,” says Zitnik. “Ageing is a very different beast. It is hard to define.”

Clock collectors

Researchers have spent decades gathering data to define that beast. One result has been a slew of ‘clocks’ aimed at measuring biological ageing, or the rate at which a person’s body exhibits signs of ageing. Such clocks measure biological age by assessing characteristics such as facial features, protein levels, gene activity and brain scans, all with the goal of quantifying whether the effects of ageing are outpacing or lagging behind someone’s chronological age in years.

How quickly are you ageing? What molecular ‘clocks’ can tell you about your health

But even as the clocks increase in sophistication, researchers are still not certain how to interpret their results. Last week, a group of researchers reported2 that an experimental drug against a lung disease had lowered the biological age of recipients in a small clinical trial. The result was based on six different ageing clocks, yet researchers struggled to conclude whether the drug truly reversed the fundamental processes of ageing, or if it merely improved overall health.

It’s a conundrum that isn’t limited to that study. “Where does ageing end, or disease start?” asks Chiara Herzog, an epigeneticist at the University of Cambridge, UK. “How do you disentangle that? It’s not really clear.”
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a significant advancement in longevity research through the development of a specialized AI system that improves understanding and measurement of biological aging. This breakthrough has broad implications for health and aging research, potentially leading to better interventions to slow aging and improve lifespan. The article provides sufficient detail on the AI system, its benchmarking, and the challenges in defining and measuring aging, highlighting its meaningful impact on the scientific community and public health.
articles.personality_title: New AI system improves how scientists measure and study aging
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists want to understand aging better to find ways to slow it down. Aging is tricky because people can have a 'biological age' that is different from their actual age, based on how their body shows signs of getting older.

**What happened** – Researchers created a special artificial intelligence (AI) system that focuses on studying aging. This system uses large language models (LLMs) trained with data about aging biology. It also includes 17 tests to check how well these AI models work for aging research. The system combines different research tools with AI helpers to make studying aging easier and more accurate.

**Impact** – This AI system helps scientists better understand biological age and how it differs from chronological age. It showed that AI models made specifically for aging research often perform better than general AI models. This is important because aging is hard to define, and this new tool sets a clearer way to study it. It could lead to better ways to measure aging and test treatments that might slow it down.

**What's next step** – Scientists will use this AI system to improve aging research and develop new AI models that understand aging even better. This could help test drugs or therapies aimed at slowing aging or improving health in old age. The system also opens the door for more detailed studies about how aging connects to diseases.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new AI system designed for aging research helps scientists measure biological age more accurately and advances the search for ways to slow down aging.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un nouveau système d'IA améliore la mesure et l'étude du vieillissement
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques cherchent à mieux comprendre le vieillissement pour trouver des moyens de le ralentir. Le vieillissement est compliqué car l’âge biologique d’une personne peut être différent de son âge réel, selon les signes physiques du corps.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs ont créé un système d’intelligence artificielle (IA) spécial qui se concentre sur l’étude du vieillissement. Ce système utilise de grands modèles de langage (LLM) entraînés avec des données sur la biologie du vieillissement. Il comprend aussi 17 tests pour vérifier l’efficacité de ces modèles dans la recherche sur le vieillissement. Le système regroupe différents outils de recherche avec des assistants IA pour faciliter et améliorer l’étude du vieillissement.

**Impact** – Ce système d’IA aide les scientifiques à mieux comprendre l’âge biologique et comment il diffère de l’âge chronologique. Il a montré que les modèles d’IA conçus spécialement pour le vieillissement fonctionnent souvent mieux que les modèles généraux. C’est important car le vieillissement est difficile à définir, et cet outil apporte une méthode plus claire pour l’étudier. Cela pourrait conduire à de meilleures mesures du vieillissement et à tester des traitements pour le ralentir.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques utiliseront ce système d’IA pour améliorer la recherche sur le vieillissement et développer de nouveaux modèles d’IA qui comprennent mieux le vieillissement. Cela pourrait aider à tester des médicaments ou thérapies visant à ralentir le vieillissement ou à améliorer la santé des personnes âgées. Le système ouvre aussi la voie à des études plus détaillées sur le lien entre vieillissement et maladies.

**Une phrase clé** – Un nouveau système d’IA dédié à la recherche sur le vieillissement aide les scientifiques à mesurer plus précisément l’âge biologique et fait avancer la recherche pour ralentir le vieillissement.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo sistema de IA mejora cómo los científicos miden y estudian el envejecimiento
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos quieren entender mejor el envejecimiento para encontrar formas de desacelerarlo. El envejecimiento es complicado porque la 'edad biológica' de una persona puede ser diferente a su edad real, según cómo muestre signos de envejecimiento su cuerpo.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores crearon un sistema especial de inteligencia artificial (IA) que se enfoca en estudiar el envejecimiento. Este sistema usa modelos de lenguaje grandes (LLM) entrenados con datos sobre biología del envejecimiento. También incluye 17 pruebas para evaluar qué tan bien funcionan estos modelos para la investigación del envejecimiento. El sistema combina diferentes herramientas de investigación con asistentes de IA para facilitar y mejorar el estudio del envejecimiento.

**Impacto** – Este sistema de IA ayuda a los científicos a entender mejor la edad biológica y cómo se diferencia de la edad cronológica. Mostró que los modelos de IA hechos especialmente para investigar el envejecimiento suelen funcionar mejor que los modelos generales. Esto es importante porque el envejecimiento es difícil de definir, y esta nueva herramienta ofrece una forma más clara de estudiarlo. Podría llevar a mejores maneras de medir el envejecimiento y probar tratamientos que lo ralenticen.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos usarán este sistema de IA para mejorar la investigación sobre el envejecimiento y desarrollar nuevos modelos de IA que entiendan mejor el envejecimiento. Esto podría ayudar a probar medicamentos o terapias para ralentizar el envejecimiento o mejorar la salud en la vejez. El sistema también abre la puerta a estudios más detallados sobre cómo el envejecimiento se relaciona con enfermedades.

**Una frase clave** – Un nuevo sistema de IA diseñado para la investigación del envejecimiento ayuda a los científicos a medir la edad biológica con más precisión y avanza la búsqueda para ralentizar el envejecimiento.
